bloks.name: STRAIGHT UP
bloks.title: How May I Help You?
bloks.dek: A quiet dignity: showing up for this, regardless.

body.text: How may I help you? is a quiet dignity — a way of saying I’m showing up for this, regardless.

“You are not here to survive. You are here to build.
You are not here to ask. You are here to decide.”
— Dr. Myles Munroe
That quote reframes this past year as training, not trials. Chasing “Finished” became: put it where it goes.

body.cap: Assume the wish is fulfilled, like Goddard said.
body.alt: Thinking GIF

body.text: How may I help you? is a play on the retail season I’m in — and a promise to myself:
Wherever I am, I’m going to show up and fix this every second of every day.

body.text: On paper, it reads like support. In practice, it’s often distance.

body.alt: Comic-style café scene: a woman in sunglasses tells a man in a hoodie, I love that for you.

body.text: “I love that for you” 💬 turned into being socially supportive while emotionally checked out.
It can mean “good for you, but I’d never touch that,” 😅 or “I don’t get it, but I won’t argue.” 🤷‍♂️
“Support” has never sounded more non-committal.
The elephant in the room
Are we…
a) cheering for each other
b) politely opting out, or
c) cutting down someone’s moment just to lift our own
Dive deeper: the origin story of the phrase, here on Instagram.

bloks.name: CHAIN REACTION
bloks.title: Declining the Stage
bloks.dek: Yonatan Sompolinsky turns down the biggest stage in crypto.

body.cap: Dr. Yonatan Sompolinsky, shown inside a world-famous meme.
body.alt: Distracted-boyfriend meme GIF with Yonatan Sompolinsky

body.text: An inflection point in crypto
Coming off last issue’s What Is a Cypherpunk, Anyway?, this week delivered the real thing — a principled bombshell that shook the crypto underworld.

On Nov 6, Dr. Yonatan Sompolinsky — one of the original researchers behind the groundbreaking Kaspa network — turned down Binance’s award naming him the #1 Independent Researcher of 2025. It would’ve put him on the same Dubai stage as Michael Saylor and “CZ” (Binance’s founder).
He declined it. Not out of ego — out of principle.
In an open letter, he thanked voters and said what most whisper:
“Crypto has shifted from a cypherpunk project to a house-friendly casino.”
His warning was sharp: when exchanges list paid-for meme coins while ignoring real decentralized innovation, they don’t just reflect the market — they steer it.
And when genuine breakthroughs get sidelined for “a green frog three weeks post-launch,” that isn’t market logic. It’s moral drift.
It wasn’t an attack. It was a wake-up call.
Decentralization isn’t price action — it’s integrity, independence, and resistance to capture.
Sompolinsky’s refusal wasn’t defiance; it was discipline.
Declining the stage may be the loudest thing he’s said to date.

bloks.name: MUSIC FLOW
bloks.title: Lykke Li — “I’m Good, I’m Gone”
bloks.dek: How one take turned into a war cry.

body.text: Picture this: it’s 2010. You stumble on to Lykke Li — soft, velvet-textured voice. Her debut single “Little Bit” lands first — shy, poppy, and magnetic.
A stellar introduction… but not the moment she became unforgettable.
Her next single, “I’m Good, I’m Gone,” is released — it still plays in shopping malls today, giving you an idea of how it started and how it’s going.
Then this happened

items: A megaphone pressed to her lips.
A one-take performance dripping with half-rehearsal / half-revolution energy.

body.text: And at the center of it, the lyrics that turned the whole room into a manifesto:

“I’m working, I sweat but it’s all good
I’m breaking my back but it’s all good

Cause I know I’ll get it back
Yeah, I know your hands will clap

Yet, I’m looking, yet, I’m working
To make butter for my piece of bun”
Translation: I’m out here, grinding for my own slice — and I’m cool with it.
There’s a mix of grit and honesty in it that still pulls me back, even now.
The live cut isn’t just a version — it’s the definitive version.

bloks.name: NOW PLAYING
bloks.title: On the Waterfront: The Glove Drop
bloks.dek: The unscripted moment we still haven’t recovered from.

body.cap: Terry Malloy and Edie Doyle in the park.
body.alt: Marlon Brando and Eva Marie Saint in a cold city park, black and white

body.text: When it comes to On the Waterfront (1954), trying to pick a single scene almost feels disrespectful — the whole film is a masterclass in performance and human truth.
But the glove-drop scene? That’s the one people still point to as the moment modern, naturalistic acting arrived.

Terry Malloy (Marlon Brando) and Edie Doyle (Eva Marie Saint) walk through a cold city park — two people who shouldn’t be together, but somehow already are. They barely know each other. She’s grieving her brother. He carries guilt he can’t say out loud. On paper, they have no business sharing a frame, let alone chemistry.
And then it happens.

body.cap: The glove drop. Watch on YouTube.
body.alt: On the Waterfront glove scene

body.text: Edie fidgets with her gloves and accidentally drops one. Everyone expected the director to yell “Cut.”
Brando didn’t even pause.

He picks it up, toys with it, slips it onto his own hand — all while keeping the conversation moving. No script direction. No planning. Just pure instinct. Suddenly the air shifts: intimacy without permission, tension without dialogue, a closeness neither character is ready to name.
That one unscripted gesture solved the whole scene

items: She isn’t ready to hold his hand.
So he “holds” her through the glove instead.

body.text: It keeps her beside him without breaking her boundaries.
Edie watches, pretending not to watch — playing off him with equal instinct. When she finally retrieves the glove, she does it in one smooth motion, no commentary. It’s all behavior, no explanation.
This is why the moment feels alive. Why actors still study it. Why it transcends the frame.
10% chaos, 90% structure.

Brando brought a small percentage of improvisation — 10% chaos, 90% structure — that forced the other actor to truly listen. Eva Marie Saint rose to meet him, and the camera just… caught something real.
Peak instinct. Peak humanity. Peak Brando.
